content.title: Response to Reviewer gws2
content.comment:
Thank you for your constructive feedback. Please find our detailed response below.

**Q1: The proposed method seems very heavy. The authors did not study the efficiency of the proposed framework.**

**A**: Thank you for pointing out this problem. Calculating featurizations used by our paper (FP, SMILES, 2D, 3D) is very efficient: computing fingerprints based on SMILES strings is almost instant. For 3D structures, there are two types of conformations involved: for pretraining, as we have access to the DFT-calculated conformations, we directly use it; for fine-tuning, as no such conformation is available, we sample conformation with RDKit which is efficient (~0.01 sec/molecule). In terms of pretraining time, our MOCO takes slightly longer than GraphMVP's. To be specific, our pretraining on GEOM-Drugs takes ~4h17m to finish whereas the baseline GraphMVP takes ~4h03m. However, to embed SMILES strings, we first pretrain a RoBERTa model on the pretraining dataset with the masking language model as the sole training objective, which takes ~2h.

**Q2: The pretraining method may be not effective. In Table 2, how to combine four featurizations in baseline method without pretraining?**

**A**. Thanks for your valuable comments. We for the first time comprehensively utilize four widely used featurization techniques for molecular representations equipped with attentive aggregation. Combining four featurizations in the baseline method would change the design scheme of the model in their original paper. For example, ContextPred [1] pretraining strategy is tailor-made for 2D graph modality, which is hard to incorporate other molecular modalities. GraphMVP[2] uses 2D-to-3D alignment, where incorporating additional featurized representations may also not be feasible.

[1] Hu et.al. Strategies for Pre-training Graph Neural Networks. ICLR 2020

[2] Liu et.al. Pre-training Molecular Graph Representation with 3D Geometry. ICLR 2022

**Q3: GraphMAE results in Table 2 are different from the original paper.**

**A**. Thanks for your careful review. We reproduce the GraphMAE results by adopting the pretrained model provided in the official github repository and report the reproduced performance to avoid unfair comparison, as all the other baseline models are fine-tuned in the same experimental settings.

**Q4: The proposed method can only learn molecule level representations. While other methods such as GNN and Transformer based methods can also generate atom level embeddings, which is useful for atom level downstream tasks.**

**A:** Thanks for your constructive comments. Actually, our architecture is also able to learn atom/node-level representations. The molecule/graph-level representations are obtained by graph pooling.

content.title: Response to Reviewer iiJx
content.comment:
Thank you for providing review for improving the clarity and the quality of our work. We have the following response for your questions.

**Q1: The main idea is somewhat incremental. These four representations do not complement each other very well.** 

**A:**  Thank you very much for your valuable comments. We agree with your statement that the graph and SMILES can be transformed into each other and FP can simply be generated using them. Actually, generating conformers (3D geometry) from graphs or SMILES are also available with the RDkit library. We would like to clarify that adding more featurizations is not our starting point. Our case studies demonstrate that single featurization together with specific encoder is deficient to properly depict the biological/chemical space to some extent. Despite the ability to generate each other, different featurizations explicitly encode differing information. We find that existing works pay much attention to the 2D graph and 3D geometry and the design of the corresponding neural encoders. Thus, we take a step forward to explore and rethink how to adaptively utilize different featurizations to complement unnoticed information.

**Q2: The technical novelty is limited. The architecture of encoders and the feature aggregation modules are borrowed from existing works and are not novel. The authors should clarify the technical contributions more clearly.**

**A**: Thanks for your valuable comment. Please refer to our general response regarding the novelty and the technical contribution of this work.

**Q3: The case studies show that different models have different capabilities for molecular representations, but cannot demonstrate that the selected modalities are complementary.**

**A**: Thank you for pointing out this problem. The case studies demonstrate that different encoders with corresponding modalities as input capture complementary information in the embedding space rather than the raw space. To validate that the learned representations are complementary to each other, we measure the similarity between each view embedding pair and report the averaged similarity scores for all molecules:

| BACE            | 2D      | 3D      | Fingerprint |
| --------------- | ------- | ------- | ----------- |
| **2D**          | -       |         |             |
| **3D**          | 0.0026  | -       |             |
| **Fingerprint** | -0.0039 | -0.027  | -           |
| **SMIELS**      | 0.0005  | -0.0026 | -0.0139     |

| HIV         | 2D      | 3D      | Fingerprint |
| ----------- | ------- | ------- | ----------- |
| 2D          | -       |         |             |
| 3D          | -0.0188 | -       |             |
| Fingerprint | -0.0233 | -0.0004 | -           |
| SMIELS      | 0.0358  | -0.0083 | -0.0396     |

From the table we conclude that all these four view embeddings contain complementary information to each other. Although SMILES, fingerprints, and 2D graphs can be converted from 3D graphs, the resulting information contained in view representations could be very different, due to the use of different encoders (each with a unique inductive bias) to extract information from each view.

**Q4: One molecule has multiple conformations, how to choose the suitable one during inference? Note that this is the key reason why 3D Informax and GraphMVP don’t use 3D information for inference.** 

**A**: Thanks for your comments. In the experiment, we use the GetConformers() API provided in RDKit library to generate a conformer for inference, which runs the distance geometry calculation from a random start point. Thus the chosen conformer is a random selection. The key reason why 3D Infomax and GraphMVP do not use 3D information for inference is that they assume the 3D structures are often very expensive to obtain, making such 3D geometric information scarce in downstream tasks. However, Jing et.al. [1] provide empirical justification for the claim that cheminformatics methods like RDKit already provide accurate local structures, which breaks the above assumption. It motivates us to leverage computationally cheap 3D information provided by RDKit during the inference stage.

[1] Bowen Jing et.al. Torsional Diffusion for Molecular Conformer Generation. NeurIPS 2022

content.comment:
I thank the authors for the thorough rebuttals and additional experiments in response to this and other reviews. The authors had given some explanations to my questions, however, the issues are not solved. I like the added similarity comparisons, but it cannot prove that these modalities are complementary. This is a trick because if you use different GNN architectures (GIN, GraphSAGE, GAT etc) to capture the information for the **same 2D graphs** and measure the similarity between the learned representations, you will also find none of them are similar.  Besides, the experimental results shown in MOCO_100K went against the usual intuition that more data is better in pre-training, raising another concern about scalability. 

Overall, I think the current manuscript studies an interesting problem. But the authors need more time to provide some in-depth comparisons and discussion to make it more solid. Therefore, I still tend to rejection.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors show that performance of molecular property prediction models is improved if they aggregate molecular representations - namely, 2D graphs, 3D graphs, Morgan fingerprints, and SMILES - into a single representation via a learned attention module. The authors demonstrate this improvement on a variety of quantum and biological property predictions tasks, and show via ablation studies that the attention module is required for this improvement. Fine-tuning the pre-trained model to a particular task and dataset is also shown to provide performance improvement.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
- The authors clearly demonstrate that the learned, aggregated molecular representation provides state-of-the-art performance on a variety of relevant tasks compared to many commonly-used property prediction models.
- The ablation studies are useful in showing that the attention head is required for the improved performance, as is using all four data input types.

Weaknesses:
- It is not obvious that the contrastive training objective used in this paper should be beneficial, since it seeks to align the learned embeddings of each input data type with their weighted average. A study that replaces this pretraining objective with something else
- In Table 2, many of the results for the best and next-best are within the standard errors of each other, weakening the claim that MOCO is state-of-the-art on these particular tasks.
- In Figure 3, it is not clear how a single attention weight was obtained, though one assumes it is by simple averaging. Making this clear in the text would help readers understand without guessing.
- In Figure 3, it is claimed that 2D input is the most influential input data type for all the toxicity tasks, however the SMILES attention weight is much larger than the 2D one for the ClinTox task. The text and discussion should be updated to reflect this fact.
- The 3D input data type seems to not contribute much to any task, including ones in which it is expected it should. This suggests that the authors might not have chosen the SchNet hyperparameters well, or trained it well, etc. The appendix explains that the authors use settings from a previous study for direct comparison. While that makes sense, the value of this study would be increased if we were convinced that the 3D graph encoder was optimal for some single task (chirality and aromatic rings study shown in Table 1).
- In section 4.3, the authors give the high dimensionality of the fingerprint representation as a reason for why it was the most important input data type in the HIV task, without further explanation. An explanation should be offered.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The work appears to be of sufficient quality, and the writing is clear.

While this reviewer is unaware of a similar published result, the results are incremental and expected. The fact that architectures and hyperparameter settings from previous studies were used in order to make the results comparable with those previous studies casts doubt on whether any strong conclusion should be drawn about the relative importance of each input data type.
content.summary_of_the_review: While the authors demonstrate that MOCO yields results at or near state-of-the-art on a variety of tasks, the results are incremental and expected. And while it is rational to conclude from this paper that using MOCO will improve model performance on property prediction tasks generally, the choice to investigate only a single contrastive objective rather than others suggests that there is additional work to be done to convince readers that this particular instantiation of MOCO should be adopted.

content.title: Response to Reviewer c1Xv (pt. 1/2)
content.comment:
Thank you for your helpful feedback. Please see our response to your concerns.

**Q1: It is not obvious that the contrastive training objective used in this paper should be beneficial, since it seeks to align the learned embeddings of each input data type with their weighted average. A study that replaces this pretraining objective with something else**

**A:** Thank you for your comments. The motivation of the contrastive objective is to adaptively distill the information contained in molecular representations resulting from diverse featurizations. Our contrastive objective is conceptually similar to contrastive knowledge distillation [1] and supervised contrastive learning [2], where the anchor instance in our paper is the aggregated molecular representation and the positive instances are all other featurized representations. The difference is that in our work, we leverage an attention network to aggregate featurized representations at first which is more flexible compared to [1] while retaining adaptive distillation ability compared to [2].

Regarding other model variants, it looks like the comments “**A study that replaces this pretraining objective with something else**” is not complete. Would you please share with us about the specific variants you are referring to? We are more than willing to conduct additional experiments for this component.

[1] Y. Tian, D. Krishnan, and P. Isola, “Contrastive Representation Distillation,” in ICLR, 2020.

[2] P. Khosla, P. Teterwak, C. Wang, A. Sarna, Y. Tian, P. Isola, A. Maschinot, C. Liu, and D. Krishnan, “Supervised Contrastive Learning,” in NeurIPS, 2020, pp. 18661–18673.

**Q2: In Table 2, many of the results for the best and next-best are within the standard errors of each other, weakening the claim that MOCO is state-of-the-art on these particular tasks.**

**A:** We separately extract the performances of the second-best baseline model and our model for comparison. The following two tables respectively compare the performances of classification tasks and regression tasks. It can be observed that our model achieves higher or comparable results. It is worth noting that the SOTA performances are extracted from different baseline models and our MOCO achieves better results overall (1.1% absolute improvement in terms of average ROC-AUC on classification tasks and 0.068 improvements in terms of RMSE on regression tasks).

|      | BBBP     | Tox21    | Toxcast  | SIDER    | ClinTox  | MUV      | HIV      | BACE     | Avg.  |
| ---- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | ----- |
| SOTA | 71.2±0.9 | 75.9±0.3 | 64.7±2.3 | 62.3±1.6 | 81.5±2.8 | 77.7±1.0 | 76.7±0.9 | 81.4±1.4 | 73.31 |
| MOCO | 71.6±1.0 | 76.7±0.4 | 64.9±0.8 | 61.2±0.6 | 81.6±3.7 | 78.5±1.4 | 78.3±0.4 | 82.6±0.3 | 74.41 |

|      | ESOL        | Lipophilicity | Malaria     | CEP         | Avg.    |
| ---- | ----------- | ------------- | ----------- | ----------- | ------- |
| SOTA | 1.091±0.021 | 0.702±0.020   | 1.101±0.015 | 1.236±0.023 | 1.03968 |
| MOCO | 0.984±0.034 | 0.707±0.001   | 1.093±0.009 | 1.101±0.007 | 0.97125 |

**Q3: In Figure 3, it is not clear how a single attention weight was obtained, though one assumes it is by simple averaging. Making this clear in the text would help readers understand without guessing.**

**A:** Thank you for your careful review. As mentioned in Section 3.1, we average the attention score of all the molecules in the same batch and apply the softmax function to scale the attention weight. We will make it clearer in the revised version for clarification.

content.title: Response to Reviewer c1Xv (pt. 2/2)
content.comment:
**Q4: In Figure 3, it is claimed that 2D input is the most influential input data type for all the toxicity tasks, however the SMILES attention weight is much larger than the 2D one for the ClinTox task. The text and discussion should be updated to reflect this fact.**

**A:** Thank you for your suggestions. We would like to clarify that SMILES is a string obtained by printing the symbol nodes with a depth-first tree traversal of a chemical graph, which means the SMILES featurization also encodes topology information as 2D graph does. The attention distribution of ClinTox dataset indicates that Roberta-based model with SMILES as input could learn better representation on the dataset than GNNs with 2D graphs as input, which also confirms the effectiveness of our adaptive learning paradigm.

**Q5: The 3D input data type seems to not contribute much to any task, including ones in which it is expected it should.**

 **A:** Thank you for bringing this issue to our attention. A 2D molecular graph implicitly defines all 3D conformers, because the set of conformers available to the molecule is implicitly defined by the molecule's identity. Essentially, the distribution of conformers is a function of the molecule itself. However, whether we are able to capture/learn that information about the conformer ensemble from a 2D/3D model, is a different question. The 3D GNN is prone to overfit its representation to the single structure it sees -- this single structure might not be representative of the overall distribution of conformers. Comparing 2D GNNs vs 3D GNNs is a question of expressive power vs. proper invariances. A 3D GNN may be more expressive, but it is quite sensitive to the particular conformation it sees. A 2D GNN is conformer-invariant by definition. Thus, we use attention machanism to realize the trade-off between expressiveness and invariance, which accounts for why 3D input data type seems to not contribute much to any task.

**Q6: In section 4.3, the authors give the high dimensionality of the fingerprint representation as a reason for why it was the most important input data type in the HIV task, without further explanation. An explanation should be offered.**

**A:** Thank you for pointing out this problem. A possible explanation for the attention weight dominated by fingerprint on HIV dataset is: the morgan fingerprint represents each atom according to a set of atomic invariants and each bit of it indicating presence or absence of specific substructures. In this way, fingerprints explicitly encode structural information with high-dimensionality which is more suitable to capture the ability of molecules to inhibit HIV replication.

content.title: Response to Reviewer SCSw
content.comment:
Thank you for your constructive feedback and encouraging comments. For your main concerns, we would like to make the following clarifications.

**Q1: It is not clear why the pretraining is only done on 50K molecules. I guess usually people use larger datasets? And I’m not sure if this work would benefit from more pretraining data.**

**A:** Thanks for your constructive reviews. Typically, there are two sets of commonly-used experimental settings for molecular pretraining: One is the setting of large-scale pretraining dataset, such as the PCQM4Mv2 [1], which contains 3M organic molecules. The other is the setting of relatively smaller pretraining dataset, such as the GEOM-Drugs, which contains 300K mid-sized molecules. Note that within GEOM-Drugs, not all molecules have at least 5 conformations. Therefore, we adopt 50K molecules,each with 5 conformers of the lowest energy, which aligns with the setting in GraphMVP and all the other pretraining baselines for a fair comparison. We further pretrain the proposed model on a larger dataset, which is twice as large as the original dataset (100K molecules) and test the performance on downstream tasks. It can be observed that the model performance improves in some tasks and decreases in others and  the average performances are basically the same.

|           | BBBP | Tox21 | SIDER | Clintox | BACE | MUV  | HIV  | ToxCase | Avg   |
| --------- | ---- | ----- | ----- | ------- | ---- | ---- | ---- | ------- | ----- |
| MOCO_50K  | 71.6 | 76.7  | 61.2  | 81.6    | 82.6 | 78.5 | 78.3 | 64.9    | 74.43 |
| MOCO_100K | 70.4 | 76.2  | 62.6  | 83.7    | 80.0 | 80.4 | 77.6 | 64.9    | 74.46 |

[1] Maho Nakata and Tomomi Shimazaki. Pubchemqc project: A large-scale first-principles electronic structure database for data-driven chemistry.

**Q2: It is not clear to me how does this model compare against the method that uses all the four features, but without pretraining. Is the first row of table 2 supposed to report this?**

**A:** Thanks for your valuable comments. Your understanding is correct. As mentioned in the subsection Baseline of the Section 4.1, we report performance with a randomly initialized multiview model as the non-pretraining baseline, which corresponds to the first row of Table 2. We will highlight this baseline setting in the paper to avoid possible confusion.

**Q3: More recent downstream tasks can be included, in addition to Table 2.**

**A:** Compared with GraphMVP, we include the same eight downstream classification tasks and four regression tasks. These downstream tasks cover three main categories: physical chemistry, biophysics, physiology. In addition, since GraphMVP did not evaluate their performance on quantum properties, we further evaluate our model on 8 quantal regression tasks of QM9 dataset to validate the effectiveness of our model and report the results in Table 3, which is aligned with another recent baseline 3D Infomax. The Alchemy dataset [1] as you pointed out is also related to quantum chemistry, so we choose the QM9 dataset which is more commonly used in the community as the downstream task. We thank you for your constructive comments and we will also do our best to supplement the performance on the Alchemy and provide timely replies.

[1] Alchemy: A Quantum Chemistry Dataset for Benchmarking AI Models

display_title: General Response: thank you & response to common concerns

content.title: General Response: thank you & response to common concerns
content.comment:
We would like to thank all reviewers very much for their extensive reviews and constructive critiques. We are encouraged that reviewers find that our approach is simple and effective (Reviewer gws2), that the advantage of the attention module is proven by ablation study (Reviewer iiJx), that the writing is clear, and that learned molecular representation provides good performance (Reviewers c1Xv and SCSw).

In the following, we would like to make clarifications regarding concerns on the novelty and technical contributions raised by reviewers:

**Q. Novelty and technical contributions**

**A**: The novelty and technical contributions of this work can be summarized from the following three aspects.

Firstly, we for the first time comprehensively utilize four widely used featurization techniques for molecular representations, covering string-, graph-, scalar-, vector-based representations for 1D/2D molecules and 3D conformation structures. We also adopt proper encoders for every featurization. Among them, since there is a lack of proper neural encoders for fingerprints, we propose an attention-based network to model interactions of feature fields in fingerprints, honoring the discrete and extremely sparse nature of fingerprint vectors. Despite the fact that other encoders are taken from existing literature, they are representative and frequently used in the community, which enables direct and fair comparison with respect to prior work. We would like to note that our proposed MOCO framework is generic and could be applied to any off-the-shelf encoders and molecular pretraining tasks.

Secondly, we propose a novel molecular pretraining framework that adaptively integrates information from multiple views in both pretraining and fine-tuning stages. This pretraining mechanism is different from all previous work (e.g., GraphCL, 3D Infomax, and GraphMVP) that only considers 2D graph structures during fine-tuning. Through extensive experiments, we empirically demonstrate that our adaptive multiview fusion involving both 1D/2D representations and 3D conformations are helpful for a variety of molecular property prediction tasks. Note that previous work has already achieved pretty high performance. For example, the current state-of-the-art GraphMAE only obtains a 1.6% absolute improvement over its best baseline in terms of average ROC-AUC. Our work pushes that boundary without extensive hyperparameter tuning, achieving a 1.1% absolute improvement over GraphMAE and 2.72% absolute improvement over GraphMVP in terms of average ROC-AUC.

Thirdly, we would like to clarify that we aim to rethink whether commonly used featurizations (e.g., 2D graph and 3D geometry) together with appropriate neural networks (e.g., GIN and SchNet) properly depict the biology and chemistry space for molecular property prediction tasks. Inspired by two simple case studies, we find that the featurizations differ in their ability to recognize different semantics. Thus, our work reveals the significance and necessity to incorporate other featurizations and corresponding encoders to complement the unnoticed information, which also leaves room for the community to reconsider the importance of different molecular modalities.

Once again, we appreciate all reviewers for their insightful suggestions which enable us to further strengthen our work. We expect that our response will resolve the reviewers' concerns. In light of our rebuttal, we sincerely hope reviewers would reply for further questions and revisit the rating.
